claim: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) and adjacent regions such as the pre- and parasubiculum are hypothesized to supply a 'spatial metric' for cognitive map-based navigation and path integration.
source: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005) and adjacent regions such as the pre- and parasubiculum (Boccara et al., 2010) are hypothesized to supply a 'spatial metric' for cognitive map-based navigation and path integration (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; McNaughton et al., 2006; Moser et al., 2017), episodic memory (Hasselmo, 2009; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014; Schiller et al., 2015), and navigating abstract feature spaces (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Hawkins et al., 2018; Rueckemann et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: Grid cells are hypothesized to support episodic memory.
source: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005) and adjacent regions such as the pre- and parasubiculum (Boccara et al., 2010) are hypothesized to supply a 'spatial metric' for cognitive map-based navigation and path integration (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; McNaughton et al., 2006; Moser et al., 2017), episodic memory (Hasselmo, 2009; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014; Schiller et al., 2015), and navigating abstract feature spaces (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Hawkins et al., 2018; Rueckemann et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on episodic memory.

claim: Grid cells are hypothesized to support navigating abstract feature spaces.
source: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005) and adjacent regions such as the pre- and parasubiculum (Boccara et al., 2010) are hypothesized to supply a 'spatial metric' for cognitive map-based navigation and path integration (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; McNaughton et al., 2006; Moser et al., 2017), episodic memory (Hasselmo, 2009; Eichenbaum and Cohen, 2014; Schiller et al., 2015), and navigating abstract feature spaces (Constantinescu et al., 2016; Hawkins et al., 2018; Rueckemann et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on abstract feature spaces.

claim: Grid cells recorded in freely foraging animals fire at multiple locations in space so that the firing fields form a hexagonal lattice.
source: Grid cells recorded in freely foraging animals fire at multiple locations in space so that the firing fields form a hexagonal lattice (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A-D showing hexagonal lattice patterns.

claim: No theory exists to date that explains the emergence of grid cell firing patterns from basic principles, unifying the many seemingly unconnected experimental observations on periodic firing patterns and their distortions in a single framework.
source: However, no theory exists to date that explains the emergence of grid cell firing patterns from basic principles, unifying the many seemingly unconnected experimental observations on periodic firing patterns and their distortions in a single framework (Jeffery, 2024; Ginosar et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent reviews noting the lack of a unifying theory.

claim: Currently existing mechanistic models of grid cell firing fall short of explaining the basic question of why grid cells exist in the first place.
source: Consequently, currently existing mechanistic models of grid cell firing fall short of explaining the basic question of why grid cells exist in the first place.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the stated lack of a unifying theory and the limitations of existing models.

claim: Oscillatory interference models and continuous attractor models provide mechanistic explanations of how the spatial periodicity in firing can emerge from the structure of microcircuits within the superficial layers of the MEC.
source: Computational models of grid cells such as oscillatory interference models (O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; Burgess et al., 2007; Giocomo et al., 2007; Hasselmo et al., 2007; Burgess, 2008) and continuous attractor models (Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Burak and Fiete, 2009; Shipston-Sharman et al., 2016) provide mechanistic explanations of how the spatial periodicity in firing can emerge from the structure of microcircuits within the superficial layers of the MEC (Zilli, 2012; Couey et al., 2013; Zutshi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to mechanistic modeling studies.

claim: Mechanistic models of grid cells cannot identify the teleological cause for the emergence of spatial periodicity in grid cell firing.
source: However, these mechanistic models, too, cannot identify the teleological cause for the emergence of spatial periodicity in grid cell firing.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the limitations of mechanistic models discussed in the text.

claim: The influential hypothesis that grid cells provide a universal map for space is challenged by experimental data suggesting a yet-to-be-identified local computational function of grid cells.
source: The influential hypothesis that grid cells provide a universal map for space is challenged by experimental data suggesting a yet-to-be-identified local computational function of grid cells (Jeffery, 2024; Ginosar et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies challenging the universal map hypothesis.

claim: This study identifies the local computational function of grid cells as a trajectory code.
source: Here, we identify this local computational function as a trajectory code.
evidence: The claim is the main assertion of the study.

claim: This study provides mathematical proof that spatial periodicity in grid cell firing emerges as the only possible solution to provide a code of trajectories in 2-D space by cell sequences.
source: In this study, we prove mathematically that spatial periodicity in grid cell firing emerges as the only possible solution to provide a code of trajectories in 2-D space by cell sequences.
evidence: The claim is the main theoretical result of the study, supported by mathematical proof presented in the manuscript.

claim: The hexagonal firing pattern of grid cells in 2-D space emerges as the most parsimonious solution with respect to the required number of neurons.
source: Within the space of all possible solutions, hexagonal symmetry in grid cell firing emerges as the most parsimonious solution with respect to the required number of neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the mathematical proof showing that seven cells are the minimum required.

claim: Cell sequences can provide a code for transitional structures of world states, generating an internal representation for memory-guided navigation.
source: This reasoning rests on well-established experimental data on neural activity in the hippocampal formation showing that cell sequences can provide a code for transitional structures of world states, generating an internal representation for memory-guided navigation (Liu et al., 2023; Buzsáki, 2010; Buzsáki et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies on cell sequences.

claim: Theta sequences of grid cell populations can provide a traveling-direction signal.
source: This reasoning rests on theoretical work demonstrating that theta sequences of grid cell populations can provide a traveling-direction signal (Zutshi et al., 2017), and that temporally structured neural activity in the hippocampal formation may be necessary to temporally bind neural representations of contiguous events (Rueckemann et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Temporally structured neural activity in the hippocampal formation may be necessary to temporally bind neural representations of contiguous events.
source: This reasoning rests on theoretical work demonstrating that theta sequences of grid cell populations can provide a traveling-direction signal (Zutshi et al., 2017), and that temporally structured neural activity in the hippocampal formation may be necessary to temporally bind neural representations of contiguous events (Rueckemann et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Data obtained from rodent experiments and theoretical work suggest that grid cells serve path integration and memory-guided navigation.
source: Moreover, data obtained from rodent experiments (Allen et al., 2014; Gil et al., 2018) and theoretical work (Sorscher et al., 2023) suggest that grid cells serve path integration and memory-guided navigation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical studies.

claim: The firing fields of grid cells must be arranged such that their centers are placed at the points of a hexagonal lattice.
source: In particular, we prove that the grid fields must be arranged such that their centers are placed at the points of a hexagonal lattice.
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof presented in the manuscript.

claim: The kissing number of a circle in the plane is 6, which is achieved using a hexagonal packing of circles.
source: The kissing number of a circle in the plane is 6, which is achieved using a hexagonal packing of circles (Thue, 1910; Fejes, 1942).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to mathematical proofs.

claim: There are five types of a lattice in the plane.
source: There are five types of a lattice in the plane (Kittel, 1966, Chapter 1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a textbook and reference to a figure.

claim: If we assume axioms 1–4, it must be the case that the intersection of all firing fields of trajectory-coding cells or all compound firing fields of cell assemblies must be congruent (the same shape), and the centers of the firing fields must be arranged in a hexagonal lattice.
source: In the following sections, we demonstrate that if we assume axioms 1–4, it must be the case that the intersecton of all firing fields of trajectory-coding cells or all compound firing fields of cell assemblies must be congruent (the same shape), and the centers of the firing fields must be arranged in a hexagonal lattice.
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof based on the stated axioms.

claim: The firing fields of trajectory-coding elements must be convex.
source: We now use Axiom 1 to demonstrate that the firing fields of trajectory-coding elements must be convex.
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof using Axiom 1.

claim: If a firing field is non-convex, a single sequence will code for more than one trajectory.
source: Examining Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, we see that if a firing field is non-convex, a single sequence will code for more than one trajectory.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to a figure demonstrating the issue with non-convex fields.

claim: Assuming axioms 1 and 4, the firing fields of trajectory-coding elements must be spatially periodic, in the sense that starting at any point and continuing in a single direction, the initial sequence of locally active elements must eventually repeat with a repeat length of at least 3.
source: More explicitly, assuming axioms 1 and 4, the firing fields of trajectory-coding elements must be spatially periodic, in the sense that starting at any point and continuing in a single direction, the initial sequence of locally active elements must eventually repeat with a repeat length of at least 3 (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Every sequence of elements along one of the three major axes of the hexagonal lattice (rows and diagonals) must be either a translation of an existent sequence in a parallel axis or consist of a disjoint set of elements.
source: First, we will demonstrate that every sequence of elements along one of the three major axes of the hexagonal lattice (rows and diagonals) must be either a translation of an existent sequence in a parallel axis or consist of a disjoint set of elements.
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof.

claim: Sequence repeats in parallel rows or diagonals must be of the same length.
source: Further, it must be true that sequence repeats in parallel rows or diagonals must be of the same length.
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof showing that different repeat lengths lead to contradictions.

claim: The length of the sequence repeat in any row or diagonal must divide the number of elements.
source: A final useful fact is that the length of the sequence repeat in any row or diagonal must divide the number of elements.
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof.

claim: The minimum number of trajectory-coding elements in 2-D space is 7.
source: Given the requirement that each firing field is surrounded by 6 firing fields of distinct elements, the minimum number of elements providing a sequence code of trajectories in 2-D space is 7.
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof based on the kissing number and axioms.

claim: There are exactly two possible arrangements of seven elements so that they form a sequence code for trajectories in 2-D space, up to relabeling of cells.
source: There are thus exactly two possible arrangements of seven elements so that they form a sequence code for trajectories in 2-D space, up to relabeling of cells.
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof examining all possible translations.

claim: Both possible arrangements of seven elements result in a hexagonal arrangement of firing fields of all distinct elements, and these arrangements are rotated against the wall of a rectangular enclosure by 10.9°.
source: Intriguingly, both possible arrangements of seven elements result in a hexagonal arrangement of firing fields of all distinct elements, and these arrangements are rotated against the wall of a rectangular enclosure by 10.9° (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is a result of the mathematical proof and is illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: Solutions with eight or more elements can result in other types of lattice packing, such as the oblique lattice or centered rectangular lattice that have also been observed in single element recordings of freely behaving animals.
source: While the two solutions to a sequence code of trajectories with seven elements both result in a hexagonal lattice packing of firing fields, solutions with eight or more elements can result in other types of lattice packing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), such as the oblique lattice or centered rectangular lattice that have also been observed in single element recordings of freely behaving animals (Stensola et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to figures and citation to experimental data.

claim: Increasing the number of elements in a sequence code does not increase the spatial or angular resolution in the representation of a trajectory.
source: Note that increasing the number of elements in a sequence code does not increase the spatial or angular resolution in the representation of a trajectory.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the properties of the sequence code.

claim: A code that uses more than the minimal number of seven elements has no functional benefit.
source: Therefore, a code that uses more than the minimal number of seven elements has no functional benefit (see 'Discussion').
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of increased resolution with more elements.

claim: The sequence code of trajectories model predicts that the spacing between two adjacent grid fields must change linearly with a change in field size.
source: Because the sequence code of trajectories model of grid cell firing implies a dense packing of firing fields, the spacing between two adjacent grid fields must change linearly with a change in field size.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the dense packing property of the model.

claim: The ratio of the field spacing to a diameter-like metric of the field size was 2.39 ± 0.25 (mean ± SD; n = 25) in experimental data from 27 grid cells recorded in mice.
source: We found that the ratio of the field spacing to a diameter-like metric of the field size was 2.39 ± 0.25 (mean ± SD; n = 25) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), which is only slightly smaller than 2.65, the upper bound predicted by the model.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ratio of grid field spacing to field size observed in experimental data is expected to be smaller than the model-predicted ratio because of factors that result in out-of-field firing of neurons recorded in experiments.
source: Note that the ratio of grid field spacing to field size observed in experimental data is expected to be smaller than the model-predicted ratio because of the many factors that result in out-of-field firing of neurons recorded in experiments, such as transient drifts of grid maps, path integration errors, conjunctive coding properties, and noise in experimental measurements (Figure 3—figure supplements 1C and 2).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on known sources of noise and variability in experimental recordings.

claim: The grid map associated with the most parsimonious solution using seven elements is rotated by 10.9° against the nearest wall of a rectangular enclosure.
source: Another testable prediction of our model is that the grid map associated with the most parsimonious solution using seven elements is rotated by 10.9° against the nearest wall of a rectangular enclosure (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is a prediction derived from the mathematical model.

claim: The 10.9° angle is well within the range of experimentally observed values, with Stensola et al., 2015 reporting a distribution of angles with a plateau between ~6 and ~12° (mean ± SD: 7.2 ± 3.5).
source: This angle is well within the range of experimentally observed values. Concretely, Stensola et al., 2015 reported a distribution of angles with a plateau between ~6 and ~12° (mean ± SD: 7.2 ± 3.5).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: The median of the angle to the nearest wall in a highly familiar as opposed to a novel environment was 9.8°.
source: Notably, the median of the angle to the nearest wall in a highly familiar as opposed to a novel environment was 9.8° (Stensola et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: Under the premise that a sequence of firing fields aligns with one of the geometric boundaries of the environment, the sequence code model explains that the grid pattern typically assumes one of only four distinct orientation configurations relative to the environment.
source: Under the premise that a sequence of firing fields aligns with one of the geometric boundaries of the environment, the sequence code model explains that the grid pattern typically assumes one of only four distinct orientation configurations relative to the environment (Stensola et al., 2015; Stensola and Moser, 2016).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model and is consistent with cited experimental observations.

claim: The four orientation configurations arise when one row of grid fields aligns with one of the two sets of parallel walls in a rectangular environment, and each arrangement can result in two distinct orientations.
source: Concretely, the four orientation configurations arise when one row of grid fields aligns with one of the two sets of parallel walls in a rectangular environment, and each arrangement can result in two distinct orientations (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the model and is illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The 2-D spatial periodicity in grid cell firing is replaced by one-dimensional (1-D) spatial periodicity if movement through space is restricted to 1-D trajectories along parallel alleys in a multicompartment maze.
source: The 2-D spatial periodicity in grid cell firing is replaced by one-dimensional (1-D) spatial periodicity if movement through space is restricted to 1-D trajectories along parallel alleys in a multicompartment maze (Derdikman et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: A sequence code of trajectories predicts fragmentation of grid cell maps in 1-D space because parallel trajectories would result in the same sequential activation of cells.
source: A sequence code of trajectories predicts such a fragmentation of grid cell maps because parallel trajectories would result in the same sequential activation of cells, and neural coding on a 1-D tract is most efficient when sequences are aligned with the movement direction (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model and is illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Grid cells have been shown to path integrate distances on a 1-D circular track.
source: Likewise, grid cells have been shown to path integrate distances on a 1-D circular track (Jacob et al., 2019), consistent with a sequence code of a trajectory along a 1-D circular track (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: Jacob et al., 2019 report that the field spacing of grid cells is increased in a 1-D circular track compared to a 2-D environment.
source: Notably, Jacob et al., 2019 report in their study that the field spacing of grid cells is increased in a 1-D circular track compared to a 2-D environment.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: An alternative explanation based on the sequence model of grid cell firing is that the animal's trajectory on a linear track is represented by a sequence of cells.
source: However, an alternative explanation based on the sequence model of grid cell firing is that the animal's trajectory on a linear track is represented by a sequence of cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model and is illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: The sequence code of trajectories is consistent with an analysis of experimental data showing that firing fields of grid cells on a 1-D linear track are compatible with a slice through a 2-D hexagonal pattern.
source: Moreover, the sequence code of trajectories is consistent with an analysis of experimental data (Pröll et al., 2018) showing that firing fields of grid cells on a 1-D linear track are compatible with a slice through a 2-D hexagonal pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data analysis.

claim: A slice through a 2-D hexagonal firing pattern explains linear-track data if translational shifts of the pattern are allowed at turning points without a requirement of rotating or scaling the grid.
source: Specifically, a slice through a 2-D hexagonal firing pattern explains linear-track data if translational shifts of the pattern are allowed at turning points without a requirement of rotating or scaling the grid.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the analysis of experimental data.

claim: A translational shift of the grid pattern of a single cell is equivalent to re-anchoring the sequence code after the animal has turned around facing the opposite direction on the linear track.
source: In the context of the sequence code of trajectories, a translational shift of the grid pattern of a single cell is equivalent to re-anchoring the sequence code after the animal has turned around facing the opposite direction on the linear track.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model.

claim: Such a translational shift or re-anchoring of the sequence code is consistent with experimental data showing differential spatial coding by place cells in the hippocampus for inbound and outbound running directions on a linear track.
source: Such a translational shift or re-anchoring of the sequence code is consistent with experimental data showing differential spatial coding by place cells in the hippocampus for inbound and outbound running directions on a linear track (Dombeck et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: Grid cells have been shown to code for traveled distance, elapsed time, or a combination of distance and time when animals run in place on a treadmill.
source: Furthermore, grid cells have been shown to code for traveled distance, elapsed time, or a combination of distance and time when animals run in place on a treadmill (Kraus et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: The firing pattern of grid cells as time or distance cells is remarkably similar to the firing pattern of grid cells that emerges when animals navigate 1-D linear tracks after correcting for logarithmic expansion in grid field size over time.
source: The firing pattern of grid cells as time or distance cells is remarkably similar to the firing pattern of grid cells that emerges when animals navigate 1-D linear tracks after correcting for logarithmic expansion in grid field size over time.
evidence: The claim is an observation based on comparison of experimental data.

claim: The fact that grid cells show repeating firing fields in other dimensions than physical space is consistent with a sequence code of trajectories in any type of dimension that has behavioral relevance for the animal.
source: The fact that grid cells show repeating firing fields in other dimensions than physical space is consistent with a sequence code of trajectories in any type of dimension that has behavioral relevance for the animal.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model and experimental observations.

claim: Experimental data by Kraus et al., 2015 demonstrate parallel coding of different dimensions by different grid cells, suggesting individual grid cell sequences can provide independent codes of trajectories through different dimensions.
source: Experimental data by Kraus et al., 2015 demonstrate parallel coding of different dimensions by different grid cells, suggesting individual grid cell sequences can provide independent codes of trajectories through different dimensions, thereby enabling parallel processing of different cognitive functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data and inference about parallel processing.

claim: Experiments in freely behaving rodents demonstrate that stretching or compression of enclosed environments results in stretching or compression of the grid map in the rescaled dimension.
source: Experiments in freely behaving rodents demonstrate that stretching or compression of enclosed environments results in stretching or compression of the grid map in the rescaled dimension. For instance, stretching or compressing the borders of a familiar open-field recording arena resulted in an increase or decrease of the distance between firing fields in the rescaled dimension of the deformed enclosure (Stensola et al., 2015; Barry et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental data.

claim: If we assume a sequence code with start and end points of trajectories anchored to landmarks or environmental borders, distortions of the grid along the rescaled dimension would be expected.
source: However, if we assume a sequence code with start and end points of trajectories anchored to landmarks or environmental borders, distortions of the grid along the rescaled dimension would be expected.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model.

claim: Experimental data in rats show that grid maps that have been established in two adjacent compartments separated by a wall within the same larger environment merge once the wall is removed.
source: Moreover, experimental data in rats show that grid maps that have been established in two adjacent compartments separated by a wall within the same larger environment merge once the wall is removed (Wernle et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: Merging of the two grid maps appeared to happen instantly, resulting in local spatial periodicity and continuity between the two original maps.
source: Merging of the two grid maps appeared to happen instantly, resulting in local spatial periodicity and continuity between the two original maps (Wernle et al., 2018), consistent with the sequence code of trajectories by grid cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: Scaling of grids has been observed in the form of an expansion, that is, increased grid spacing between individual firing fields and increased field sizes, in response to novelty of the environment.
source: Scaling of grids has also been observed in the form of an expansion, that is, increased grid spacing between individual firing fields and increased field sizes, in response to novelty of the environment (Barry et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: Scaling of grids has been reported in climbing rats foraging on a vertical wall.
source: Such scaling has also been reported in climbing rats foraging on a vertical wall (Casali et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: Both the scaling of grids in response to scaling the borders of an environment and the expansion of grid fields in response to novelty are inconsistent with the hypothesis that grid cells provide a spatial metric for navigation or path integration.
source: Both the scaling of grids in response to scaling the borders of an environment and the expansion of grid fields in response to novelty are inconsistent with the hypothesis that grid cells provide a spatial metric for navigation or path integration.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the incompatibility of the observations with the spatial metric hypothesis.

claim: An increase in grid spacing in response to a novel environment can be explained by a sequence code of trajectories reflecting an initially broader spatial resolution.
source: However, an increase in grid spacing in response to a novel environment can be explained by a sequence code of trajectories reflecting an initially broader spatial resolution.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model.

claim: Experimental data show that changes in grid field size co-occur, though to a lesser extent, with changes in the size of place cell firing fields in response to novel environments.
source: While this hypothesis needs to be tested in future studies, experimental data show that changes in grid field size co-occur, though to a lesser extent, with changes in the size of place cell firing fields in response to novel environments (Barry et al., 2012; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Karlsson and Frank, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental data.

claim: A sequence code of trajectories in 2-D space is consistent with experimental data showing that grid fields move toward goal locations.
source: Furthermore, a sequence code of trajectories in 2-D space is consistent with experimental data showing that grid fields move toward goal locations (Boccara et al., 2019) or restructure their spatial firing maps to incorporate the location of a learned reward (Butler et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental data.

claim: Experimental data show that grid fields restructure their spatial firing maps to incorporate the location of a learned reward.
source: Furthermore, a sequence code of trajectories in 2-D space is consistent with experimental data showing that grid fields move toward goal locations (Boccara et al., 2019) or restructure their spatial firing maps to incorporate the location of a learned reward (Butler et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: These data support the hypothesis that grid cells do not provide a simple metric of space.
source: These data support the hypothesis that grid cells do not provide a simple metric of space.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the cited experimental data showing malleability of grid maps.

claim: The spatial firing pattern of grid cells is malleable in response to relevant contextual features.
source: Instead, the spatial firing pattern of grid cells is malleable in response to relevant contextual features.
evidence: The claim is an inference from experimental data showing grid map distortions.

claim: Local distortions of global grid patterns by salient locations have recently been compared to spacetime distortions by blackholes.
source: Such local distortions of global grid patterns by salient locations have recently been compared to spacetime distortions by blackholes (Ginosar et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Warping of grid maps is caused by an increased probability that the currently active grid cell activates the next grid cell in the sequence of trajectory-coding cells, resulting in the center of firing fields moving closer together.
source: We propose that such warping of grid maps is caused by an increased probability that the currently active grid cell activates the next grid cell in the sequence of trajectory-coding cells, resulting in the center of firing fields moving closer together.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the sequence code model.

claim: A reduction of the spacing between spatial fields has been observed in hippocampal place fields, resulting in a backward shift with experience.
source: A reduction of the spacing between spatial fields has been observed in hippocampal place fields, resulting in a backward shift with experience (Mehta et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2004; Roth et al., 2012; Geiller et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2021) due to NMDA receptor-dependent plasticity (Ekstrom et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental data.

claim: Under the premise that the grid map is anchored to the reward site, this would result in a progressive decrease in grid spacing toward the reward site, thereby causing local distortions in the grid map of a single grid cell.
source: Under the premise that the grid map is anchored to the reward site, this would result in a progressive decrease in grid spacing toward the reward site, thereby causing local distortions in the grid map of a single grid cell (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model and is illustrated in Figure 4E.

claim: A sequence code of trajectories by grid cells is consistent with malleable grid maps because the spacing between adjacent firing fields can change in response to local contextual features without compromising the sequence code.
source: A sequence code of trajectories by grid cells is thus consistent with malleable grid maps because the spacing between adjacent firing fields can change in response to local contextual features without compromising the sequence code.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model.

claim: The same mechanism can explain shearing-induced asymmetry and multiple alignment solutions that have been shown in experimental data.
source: The same mechanism can explain shearing-induced asymmetry and multiple alignment solutions that have been shown in experimental data (Stensola et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model and is consistent with cited experimental data.

claim: The definition of sequence coding of trajectories implies that each grid cell's collection of firing fields is geometrically congruent to any other grid cell's collection of firing fields.
source: In addition to properties of grid cell firing on the single cell level, the definition of sequence coding of trajectories implies an intriguing property of grid cells on the population level, namely that each grid cell's collection of firing fields is geometrically congruent to any other grid cell's collection of firing fields.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the definition of sequence coding of trajectories.

claim: This property mirrors experimental data from single-element recordings in rodents showing that adjacent firing field grid patterns of different anatomically close grid cells differ only in phase but have the same orientation and scale.
source: This property mirrors experimental data from single-element recordings in rodents showing that adjacent firing field grid patterns of different anatomically close grid cells differ only in phase but have the same orientation and scale (Hafting et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental data.

claim: The sequence code of trajectories model accounts for smooth transitions between firing fields and the representations of more than six running directions by using multiple grids of seven elements each, where each element has the same field size but the firing fields are shifted in phase.
source: Consistent with experimental data (Hafting et al., 2005), the sequence code of trajectories model of grid cell firing accounts for smooth transitions between firing fields and the representations of more than six running directions by using multiple grids of seven elements each, where each element has the same field size. However, the firing fields are shifted in phase.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the sequence code model and is consistent with cited experimental data.

claim: One needs to add three grids composed of the same number of elements as the original grid and shifted in phase such that their field centers fall exactly between the firing fields along one major axis of the original grid.
source: It follows from Axiom 3 that one needs to add three grids composed of the same number of elements as the original grid and shifted in phase such that their field centers fall exactly between the firing fields along one major axis of the original grid (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is an inference from Axiom 3 and is illustrated in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The firing fields of all distinct elements of the compound grid must again fall on a hexagonal lattice.
source: Consequently, the firing fields of all distinct elements of the compound grid must again fall on a hexagonal lattice.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the properties of the sequence code model.

claim: An arbitrarily smooth transition between grid fields/grid cells becomes possible during navigation with an arbitrarily large number of grid cells (organized in fundamental grids of seven elements with non-overlapping firing fields).
